paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Reformation, also called the Protestant Reformation, was a great religious movement inside Western Christianity in 16th-century Europe. It challenged the pope and the leaders of the Catholic Church, both on matters of belief and on matters of power. Coming near the close of the Renaissance, it marked the birth of Protestantism. Historians count it among the events that ended the Middle Ages and began the early modern period in Europe.

paragraphs.heading: When it started and ended
paragraphs.text: Most accounts start the story in 1517, when Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses, the work that gave rise to Lutheranism. The usual date is 31 October 1517, when Luther is said to have nailed this paper on indulgences and papal power to the castle church door in Wittenberg. Calvinist historians often prefer 1516, when the Swiss priest Huldrych Zwingli first preached against abuses in the Church. The end is argued over even more; common choices are the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 and the start and end of the Thirty Years' War in 1618 and 1648.

paragraphs.heading: Faith alone
paragraphs.text: In general, the Reformers held that justification rests on faith in Jesus Christ alone, while the Catholic view joined faith with the charitable acts that grow from it. For Lutherans, Anglicans and the Reformed, good works were the fruit of a living faith and belonged to sanctification, a separate process from justification. Protestant groups broadly agreed on points now summed up as the three solae. Yet they split on other matters, such as how Christ is present in the Eucharist: Lutherans saw a bodily presence, the Reformed a spiritual one.

paragraphs.heading: How it spread
paragraphs.text: Gutenberg's printing press let religious writings spread quickly in the languages people actually spoke. The movement began in Saxony, in Germany, and then branched out. Nearby, the Swiss Zwingli and the Frenchman John Calvin shaped the Continental Reformed tradition. Thomas Cranmer led the change in England and John Knox in Scotland, giving rise to Anglicanism and Presbyterianism. The same years also saw Radical Reformers such as the Anabaptists, who wanted to go back to the ways of the earliest Christians.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word Protestant came from
paragraphs.text: The first people called Protestants were six princes of the Holy Roman Empire and the rulers of fourteen Imperial Free Cities. In 1529 they formally objected to an order issued by the Diet of Speyer. That order took back concessions to the Lutherans that Emperor Charles V had approved three years before. At first the word was purely political, but later it came to mean a member of any Western church that held to the main Reformation principles.

paragraphs.heading: Answer and aftermath
paragraphs.text: The Catholic Church replied with the Counter-Reformation, in which the Council of Trent cleared up disputed teachings and dealt with abuses the reformers had attacked. The wars of religion that followed across Europe killed between seven and seventeen million people. Since the late 20th century, many historians speak of Reformations in the plural. They want to stress that it was not one tidy event but several movements running side by side.
